name: Uma Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Uma, thanks for doing this. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead operator in the machining cell at Hartley Furniture. We make kitchen cabinet doors and drawer fronts. I run the CNC router, a machine that cuts wood panels from a digital drawing, and the edge-bander that glues the trim on. I load the programs, set the cutters, and check the first door of every batch with a square and my thumb. I've got two operators under me and a lot of sawdust in my hair.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, mostly on my phone. When a customer wants an odd door, I ask the AI to help me adjust the cutting program, and then I check every line, because it makes mistakes. At home I use it to price the shelves I build on weekends in my dad's garage. Hartley doesn't know about the AI. They just know my changeovers are fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype, then. I'd be a little bit sorry, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's handy but no miracle, which is what I've found myself. At work I'd say keep learning anyway, it saves you time. At church I'd say good, we can all calm down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'm still on low pay at Hartley with about two weeks of money saved. I rent a room from an older lady near my parents, which is cheap but not a home. Hartley's orders dip every January and they put us on four days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Hartley because it's the only furniture factory near here. I'd grow the weekend shelving, I've got four orders for Christmas already, and try to get it to three hundred a month. And I'd save that money toward a small CNC machine of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless, but hopeful. I like having something that's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said four days in January. How do you get through that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I take more shelving jobs, and Dad lets me use his garage for free. My mum feeds me on Sundays. That's how my family does it, we help each other out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would a small CNC machine cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decent desktop one is about two thousand. That's most of a year of weekends. But with my own CNC machine, I could make in a day what takes me a weekend by hand.

say: AI is **handy, no miracle**, which matches her own experience.
People should **keep learning** it anyway because it saves time.
think: She's still on **low pay** with about two weeks saved.
Hartley puts staff on **four days** every January.
do: Keep working at **Hartley**, the only furniture factory nearby.
Grow **weekend shelving** to three hundred a month.
Save toward a **two-thousand** desktop CNC machine.
feel: **Restless** but **hopeful**, liking something of her own.
S0.quote: With my own CNC machine, I could make in a day what takes me a weekend by hand.
fieldNote: She is **entrepreneurial**, using AI for both work and side business.
Family provides **free workspace** and meals, which she sees as normal.
Her real pressure is **January short weeks** and low pay.

steps.text: Keep running the CNC router and edge-bander at Hartley
Build shelving orders to three hundred a month
Save toward a two-thousand desktop CNC machine

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first. Okay, that I can use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say anyone who learns the tools will do fine, and anyone who waits for someone to rescue them won't. At work I'd show the lads how I use it for programs. Online I'd share my shelf designs, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it cuts both ways. AI makes my side business much easier, from drawings to pricing to answering customers. But Hartley's office would shrink, and if they buy a fully automatic panel line, my cell needs one person, not three. I'd want to be that one person, or my own boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the small CNC machine within the year, even on a payment plan. I'd use AI for the customer side of the shelving, quotes and emails, so I can do more orders. And I'd tell Hartley I want to learn any new automatic line first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at work, excited at home. Both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a payment plan. With two weeks of savings, is that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. If January's bad and the orders dry up, I'd be paying for a machine I can't use. My dad would back me for a month or two, but I wouldn't want to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your two operators do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leon would be fine, he's good with screens. Gary is fifty and slow with new things. I'd try to get Hartley to keep Gary on the edge-bander as long as it's there.

She'd **show colleagues** her AI programming method.

do: Buy the **small CNC** machine this year on a payment plan.
Use AI for **quotes and emails** on the shelving business.
Ask to learn any new **automatic line** first.
S1.quote: Anyone who learns the tools will do fine, and anyone who waits for someone to rescue them won't.
fieldNote: She takes a **real risk** with a machine on credit and thin savings.
She still wants to **protect Gary**, an older operator.

steps.text: Buy a desktop CNC machine on a payment plan
Use AI to write quotes and customer emails for shelving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking part. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should stop waiting for the government and start building something for themselves. But I'd also say firms like Hartley should give staff notice and a chance to buy old machines cheap. That's fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, by 2028 the AI can draw and program anything, so my edge goes. By 2031 robots load and run the router. My hands-on skill has three years left at Hartley. The only thing that lasts is what I own and who I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave Hartley in the second year and go full-time on fitted shelving and small kitchen jobs, using AI for all the design. I'd move back in with my parents to cut rent. And I'd ask Hartley if I could buy one of their old edge-banders when they automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd rather be moving than sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would people still pay you, if AI and robots can do it all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in ten years they won't. But in 2029, people still want someone to come round, measure their crooked old walls and fit it right. Old houses aren't square, and the robots won't be in people's kitchens yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would say finally, you're your own boss. Mum would say what about a pension. They'd both be right.

say: People should **stop waiting** for government and build something themselves.
Firms should give **notice** and let staff buy old machines cheap.
think: By 2028 AI **programs anything**, so her edge goes.
Only **what she owns** and who she knows lasts.
do: **Leave Hartley** in year two to fit shelving full-time.
**Move back** with her parents to cut rent.
Ask to **buy an old edge-bander** from Hartley.
feel: **Anxious**, but would rather be **moving** than still.
S2.quote: Old houses aren't square, and the robots won't be in people's kitchens yet.
fieldNote: She sees **fitting in old homes** as a gap robots won't fill soon.
Self-employment is a **bet** made with no savings and family backing.
Her views blend **self-reliance** with a call for fair treatment by firms.

steps.text: Leave Hartley in year two to fit shelving full-time
Move back in with her parents to cut rent
Buy an old edge-bander from Hartley when it automates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's long enough to build the business properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great time to start something, if you're willing to work. I'd say young people should look at trades where you go into people's homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's close to ideal. Five years to grow the shelving into a real business, with the thinking AI doing my drawings and quotes from 2031, while I keep the steady wage at Hartley until 2033. Then I go when the robots come in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the desktop CNC next spring with cash, not credit. I'd register the business properly and get insurance. And I'd do a short course on fitting kitchens, so I can take bigger jobs than shelves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about Hartley, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of building a business with thin savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saying no to work at Hartley's overtime so I've got weekends free. Every weekend I build shelves, I'm not earning time and a half. That's a real choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change in your personal life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd finally get a flat of my own, in about three years, once the business pays. I'd like to have a place to bring someone home to, honestly.

say: It's a **great time** to start something, if you'll work.
Young people should look at **trades in homes**.
think: Five years is **close to ideal** for growing the business.
She'd keep **Hartley's wage** until 2033, then go when robots come.
do: Buy the **desktop CNC** next spring with cash.
S3.quote: Every weekend I build shelves, I'm not earning time and a half.
fieldNote: She plans precise **timing**: AI tools from 2031, leave Hartley before robots.
The key trade-off is **overtime versus weekends** on her business.
She hopes for **a flat of her own** and a partner.

steps.text: Buy the desktop CNC machine next spring with cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a whole career's head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who complains has a decade to do something. I'd say it kindly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's good. I'd build the business slowly, keep Hartley's wage, and by 2036 I'd be using AI for all the design and paperwork. By 2039 I might buy a small robot myself. The robots coming could be my staff, not my replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at Hartley and grow the shelving at weekends, saving a hundred a month. I'd buy the CNC machine in a year or two. And I'd move into a flat of my own once the business pays the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Proper calm, like I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a small robot of your own. Can you picture that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot arm that sands and finishes doors while I'm out fitting. That would double what I can make. If the price comes down, why not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could get ill, or a big company could sell fitted kitchens with robot fitters cheaper than me. Then I'd change again. But ten years is plenty of time to see it coming.

She'd say it **kindly**, but she'd say it.
think: The **robots** could be her staff, not her replacement.
By 2036 she'd use **AI** for all design and paperwork.

Save **a hundred** a month and buy the CNC in a year or two.
Move into **her own flat** once the business pays rent.

S4.quote: The robots coming could be my staff, not my replacement.
fieldNote: The long warning makes her see **automation as opportunity**.

steps.text: Grow weekend shelving while staying at Hartley

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to jump with two weeks of savings and no business built yet. What would help is small start-up loans for tradespeople, cheap and quick, and the chance to buy old factory machines when firms automate. Not benefits, just a fair start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who'll train the next lot. I learned from an old cabinet maker called Frank at Hartley. If the robots take the factory floor, nobody will learn the trade the way I did.

headlineQuote: Not benefits, just a fair start.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old** CNC router lead at Hartley Furniture, making kitchen cabinet doors.
She rents a room near her parents, with about **two weeks** saved and short weeks every January.
**Traditional** and self-reliant, she leans on family and dislikes waiting for government help.
She uses **AI daily** for programs and pricing, and runs a weekend shelving business.
Every scenario pushes her toward **her own business**; only the two-year warning makes her anxious.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: jumping with **two weeks** of savings and no business built.
whatWouldHelp: The chance to **buy old machines** when factories automate.
